summary.text: Manorialism was the method of land ownership in parts of Europe, notably France and later England, during the Middle Ages.
A lord and his dependents lived in a manor house or castle and ran a rural estate, while labourers or serfs worked the surrounding land to support themselves and the lord.
It was part of the feudal system, and it was slowly replaced by a money-based market economy and new forms of agrarian contract.

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: Seigneurialism, the manor system or manorial system

facts.label: Roman roots
facts.value: Originated in the Roman villa system of the Late Roman Empire

facts.label: How labour paid
facts.value: Labour time or produce first, then cash payment

facts.label: Last feudal dues
facts.value: Abolished in France at the French Revolution

facts.label: Church lords
facts.value: Bishops and abbots held lands with similar obligations

items.prompt: In the early Middle Ages a farm worker hands part of his harvest to the lord. Centuries later, his descendant pays the lord in coins instead. What lies behind the change?

options.label: Growing commercial activity
Lords no longer needed food once they left their manors
Farm work was no longer needed on the estate
Churches took over all grain collection from lords

items.explain: Labourers first paid with labour time or produce, and later paid in cash as commercial activity increased.

items.prompt: A historian looks for the ancestor of the medieval manor system. Where do its antecedents lead?

options.label: The longhouses of Viking settlers
The city-states of ancient Greece
The rural economy of the later Roman Empire
The courts of early Islamic caliphs

items.explain: Manorialism originated in the Roman villa system, and its antecedents can be traced to the rural economy of the later Roman Empire.

items.prompt: Late Roman officials froze society in place: sons followed their fathers' trades, and cultivators could not leave the land they were attached to. Where was this heading for the workers of the land?

options.label: They were on their way to owning land outright
They were on their way to serving as paid soldiers
They were on their way to running market towns
They were on their way to becoming serfs

items.explain: Because cultivators were tied to the land, the workers of the land were on their way to becoming serfs.

items.prompt: Serfs are gone from an estate, yet the lord still runs it with freehold labourers. What does this show about the manor system?

options.label: It had already vanished with the serfs
It could carry on after serfdom ended
It had turned into a military order
It could only work on royal land

items.explain: Manorialism outlasted serfdom in the sense that it continued with freehold labourers.

items.prompt: Which sight in the countryside was the most vivid feature of manorialism, and faded away along with it?

options.label: The open field system, with strips of land worked individually
Stone aqueducts carrying water to each village
Walled monasteries standing beside every estate
Rows of watchtowers along every border

items.explain: Manorialism faded slowly alongside its most vivid feature in the landscape, the open field system, where strips of land were individually worked.

items.prompt: An abbey holds a seigneurie, and a bailiff handles much of its business. What does this show about who could be a lord and how a lord's power worked?

options.label: Only individual nobles could be lords, and always ruled in person
Only the king could be a lord, and bailiffs held no power
A lord could be an institution, and power ran through intermediaries
Lords were chosen by villagers, who then picked a bailiff

items.explain: A lord could be an individual or an ecclesiastical institution such as an abbey, and the lord's power was exercised through intermediaries, most importantly the bailiff.
